about: Each session's default run of show, for a 75-minute session. Each entry in `weeks` is one session (week 0 is Prep), and the site seeds a new cohort's sessions from this file, and every scene stays editable in the class builder. Scenes use the site's shape (assets/show-lib.js on the site branch): kind, title, minutes, body (what the main stage shows), and config. Written by Claude from docs/research/curriculum/00-curriculum-design.md, October 7, 2026, awaiting Ben's review. A scene's optional `note` is for the teacher only, and a week's `questions` go into the cohort's question bank (kind, prompt, choices, points).

weeks.title: Cohort Prep: getting set up and meeting your group
weeks.question: What do I need in order to build at all?

scenes.title: Arrive
scenes.body: Your name, and in one sentence, what you want your app to do for someone you know.

scenes.title: How we talk to one another
scenes.body:
The four rules, said aloud.

And one true story about a rough first week.

scenes.title: Meet your group
scenes.body: Groups of three. Each person opens their app's address on their phone and shows it.

config.prompt: Show your app's address on your phone, and say one thing in your life you wish worked differently.

room_scenes.title: Show the address on your phone
One thing you wish worked differently

scenes.note: Watch for anyone whose setup is still stuck, and anyone who has not met their trio yet.

scenes.title: A strong bring-back and a weak one
scenes.body: Both shown, then everyone practices the three questions on the weak one, on the board.

scenes.title: Start your noticing log
scenes.body:
For five days, write one line whenever one of these happens:

I wished something worked differently.
I gave up on something I care about.
I did something the long way because nothing helped.
Someone I know struggled with the same thing.

No app ideas yet. Just what happened.

config.prompt: What is one thing that happened today that could go in your log?
What do you hope this app will do for someone?
How ready do you feel to build?

questions.prompt: What do you hope this app will do for someone?
How ready do you feel to build?
What did your agent do for you during setup that you expected to have to do yourself?
Where will you keep your noticing log this week?
choices: A notes app on my phone

weeks.title: Week 1: finding a problem worth building for
weeks.question: What problem in your own life is worth building something for, and who else has it?

scenes.title: Arrive
scenes.body:
One line in the chat from your noticing log, one you are willing to share.

Then what I heard in last week's answers, and what I changed because of it.

scenes.title: Two notes for one film
scenes.body:
Two notes for the same film in Archive Watch, side by side.

One was written in a second by an AI. The other was written by someone who watched the film and shared it on archive.org.
scenes.note: Prepare these before the session: copy one film's notes from its archive.org page, and ask your agent for a three-sentence summary of the same film. Label them A and B, and do not say which is which until people have answered.

config.prompt: Which would you rather read, and what would be lost if the app only had the first kind?

scenes.title: Our questions
scenes.body:
Ask as many questions as you can.

Do not stop to discuss, judge, or answer them.

Write each one down exactly as it was said.

Change any statement into a question.

config.prompt: If anyone can build their own apps, it matters even more which apps they choose to build. What questions does that raise for you?

scenes.note: These are the Question Formulation Technique's four rules (Right Question Institute). Collect every question in the session's thread. They become the cohort's list of what we need to know, and you come back to it every week.

scenes.title: Five from your log
scenes.body: With your agent closed, choose five lines from your log and write each as a problem, in your own words, one or two sentences each.

config.prompt: Which five things in your log would you most like to be different?

scenes.title: Hold them to the tests
scenes.body: Put your two strongest on the board. For each test, mark yes, not yet, or I don't know. "I don't know" is an honest answer, and it is what this week's conversations are for.
scenes.note: Watch for a problem that is really a measurement or a ranking, with nobody's story in it, and ask about it with a question, not a verdict.

scenes.title: What makes a problem statement strong
scenes.body:
Four problems I wrote, in my own words. Each starts from a real situation in my life, says what a better life would look like, and then says "I need something that..."

Read them as models, not answers. What do they do that you could do in yours?

config.prompt: In a few words, what do these four problem statements do well?

scenes.title: Rewrite yours
scenes.body:
Rewrite your strongest candidate in the same form: what happens in your life, then "I need something that..."

Then one sentence on what the computer-shaped version of the same wish would be, so you can see what to steer away from.

config.prompt: What happens in your life, and what do you need?

scenes.title: Critique in your trio
scenes.body: Groups of three. Be kind, be specific, be helpful, and offer suggestions as questions: "Have you considered...?"

config.prompt: Read your problem statement aloud. Then listen to the questions, and write down the one you want to answer.

scenes.note: Critique rules from Ron Berger. Watch for a statement that names a technology instead of a situation, and for a room where nobody asks a question.

scenes.title: Plan two conversations
scenes.body: Name two people who might have this problem too. Write three questions that start "Tell me about the last time you..." Do not describe an app.

config.prompt: Who are your two people, and what is your first question for them?
How sure are you, right now, that someone besides you has this problem?
What is still muddy?

questions.prompt: Which would you rather read, and what would be lost if the app only had the first kind?
In a few words, what do these four problem statements do well?
How sure are you, right now, that someone besides you has this problem?
What is still muddy?
Which of these does your problem statement do?
choices: Starts from something that happens in my life
Says what a better life would look like

questions.prompt: Which questions for your two conversations will tell you the most?
choices: Tell me about the last time you...

weeks.title: Week 2: the first app, and the same app on a second device
weeks.question: What has to be the same on every device, and what should feel as if it was born there?

scenes.title: Arrive
scenes.body:
One line in the chat: what the person you talked to did first with your app.

Then what I heard in last week's answers, and what I changed because of it.

scenes.title: Show what you brought back
scenes.body: Groups of three, about ten minutes each. Your problem statement, then the app on your phone.

config.prompt: Read your problem statement, show the app on your phone, and say what the person you talked to did first.

scenes.note: Watch for a problem statement that has not changed since week 1, "my friend liked it" with nothing about what the person did, and a first version that grew past the smallest thing.

scenes.title: What surprised us
scenes.body: One or two people: what a real person did with your app that you did not expect.

config.prompt: Listen for what the person did that the builder did not plan for.

scenes.title: Where Archive Watch went next
scenes.body:
Apple TV on April 17, where its people were. iPhone and iPad, the web, and Android on June 9. Mac on June 22. Roku on September 3.

Use the order as a model, not an answer: where do the people you talked to already reach?

config.prompt: Which device will the people you talked to reach for, and why that one second?

scenes.title: One verb, twice
scenes.body:
The one thing your app must do everywhere, drawn twice: the way it works on your first platform, and the way it should feel on the second, with that device's own controls.

Partners write one question beside each drawing.

scenes.title: Start
scenes.body: Write the one verb that must be the same everywhere, and one rule about your data. Then send the first prompt of stage 02.

config.prompt: What is the first prompt you will send this week?
Which of these belong in the data, so every platform gets them the same way? Choose every one.
options: The size of the play button

config.prompt: What is still muddy?

questions.prompt: Which device will the people you talked to reach for, and why that one second?
Which of these belong in the data, so every platform gets them the same way? Choose every one.
choices: The size of the play button

questions.prompt: What is still muddy?

weeks.title: Week 3: proof that it works, and someone else's hands
weeks.question: How do I know it works, and what happens when someone I did not build it with holds it?

scenes.title: Arrive
scenes.body:
One line in the chat: the one cell your own eyes proved wrong this week.

Then what I heard in last week's answers, and what I changed because of it.

scenes.title: Show what you brought back
scenes.body: Groups of three, about ten minutes each. Two devices in hand where you can.

config.prompt: Show one verb on both platforms, the cell your eyes proved wrong, and your app's look beside the template's.

scenes.note: Watch for a second platform that only runs in a simulator, a look with no line back to the people it is for, and anyone who has not named a person outside the cohort whose device the app could reach.

scenes.title: Read one real prompt
scenes.body: A classmate's stuck moment, with their permission, or the doubled-up feed from stage 04. Write the prompt you would send before you see the real one.

scenes.title: Watching someone hold it
scenes.body: Give one person one thing to do with your app. Then watch, without explaining, and write down what they did, where they paused, and what they said, in their words.

scenes.title: Start
scenes.body: Ask your agent to prove its next fix on your device. Then plan who will hold your app, on which device, and how it gets there for free.

config.prompt: Who will hold it, on which device, and how will it get there?

scenes.title: What do you ask to see?

config.prompt: When your agent says something is fixed, what do you ask to see, and why is its word not enough?
What is still muddy?

questions.prompt: When your agent says something is fixed, what do you ask to see, and why is its word not enough?
How do you know your last fix is real?
What is still muddy?

weeks.title: Week 4: the app on someone else's device
weeks.question: What happens when someone I did not build it with holds it?

scenes.title: Arrive
scenes.body:
One line in the chat: shipped or stuck.

Then what I heard in last week's answers, and what I changed because of it.

scenes.title: Show what you brought back
scenes.body: Groups of three, about ten minutes each. I will visit every group tonight.

config.prompt: Show the app on someone else's device, or tell us what they said.

scenes.note: Watch for anyone who has not published to another person yet, and visit every group.

scenes.title: One value at work
scenes.body: One decision a value changed this week, and what it cost. Then the one thing I heard across groups.

config.prompt: Listen for the value at work, and what it cost.

scenes.title: Write, play, publish, this week
scenes.body: Fill in your own week: what you wrote, what you played with, and who you published to.

scenes.title: Start
scenes.body: Write down one thing you wanted from your own use of the app this week.

config.prompt: What is the first prompt you will send this week?
Rank what the other person noticed first.
In one word, how did it feel to hand it over?

questions.prompt: Rank what the other person noticed first.
In one word, how did it feel to hand it over?
What is one thing about your app you can no longer see by using it yourself, and how will you find out about it?

weeks.title: Week 5: a feature you wanted, shown to everyone
weeks.question: What did I learn that the next builder should not have to, and is this version enough for its people?

scenes.title: Arrive
scenes.body:
Guests, welcome.

The four rules, said once more, for everyone. Then what I heard in last week's answers.

scenes.title: Show what you brought back
scenes.body: Groups of three, one last time, about six minutes each.

config.prompt: Explain every part of your app, even the parts the agent wrote.

scenes.note: Watch for whether each student can name what is enough, for now.

scenes.title: The showing
scenes.body: Everyone, about two minutes each: the feature you wanted, and one value with the decision it changed.

config.prompt: Guests may ask one question each. Listen for what is enough, for now.

scenes.title: The three questions, on the showing
scenes.body: Where is it going, how is it going, and what is next, for the apps you just saw.

scenes.title: Start
scenes.body: The cohort chooses its one lesson to send back to the template. Then everyone sends the first prompt of whatever comes next.

config.prompt: What is the first prompt of whatever comes next?
What waits for the next version?
What is still muddy?

questions.prompt: What waits for the next version?
What is still muddy?
What will your agent know at the start of your next app that it did not know in week 1, and where does that knowledge live?
